tasks.task: The owner set the water bar on 14 Nov 2026 as shipped high-end games: "Scenery reflections we must have, that's a main stay in high quality modern games. That's the standard we're after. Camera being able to go under water we need to support as well." The WATERS re-plan of that day left out caustics, underwater light shafts and exposure that adapts under water, which are standard in high-end underwater views; bring the underwater view up to that bar in WATERS (or the owning module), and plan the new module SCENE-VIEWS that WATERS M14 depends on. Choose methods from first principles and current practice. Do not change WATERS M1, which is being built.

The second design reviews of SCENE-VIEWS and RIVERS (docs/evidence/SCENE-VIEWS/design-review.md, docs/evidence/RIVERS/design-review.md) each found 1 Must Fix. Resolve both in the designs and plans, keeping them consistent with WATERS, PUDDLES and ATMOSPHERE. Suggestions are yours to take or leave; say which you took and why.

Two tasks in one pass.
1) Dependency audit. The owner (14 Nov 2026) says development is far behind pace: Codex quota use is about 5% a day against a target near 15%, because only 4 milestones can start at once. Go through every milestone dependency in docs/plans/*/PLAN.md and DONE.json, and remove each edge that only sets an order, keeping only those where a milestone needs another milestone's actual output (code, interface, data or a verified baseline it builds on). Where a milestone needs only part of another, depend on the earliest milestone that provides that part. Owner decision: keep the swarm-game modules (SIM-2D, SWARM, TRANSPORT, RENDER-2D, GAME-UI, SESSION) gated on SHOWCASE:M8 as they are now. Contention for the shared GPU lock and disk is not a reason for an edge; the script queues GPU work. List each edge you removed or kept with a one-line reason in the evidence folder, and say how many milestones can start once the running ones finish.
2) ATMOSPHERE's latest design review (docs/evidence/ATMOSPHERE/design-review.md) found 1 Must Fix after the horizon-haze re-plan. Resolve it, keeping SCENE-VIEWS, WATERS and CLOUDS consistent.

Move Thrum onto the proof regime the owner approved, using orchestrate 2.3.1, in one pass, tonight.

Why: delivery stalled under proofs. In the last 24h, 4 milestones reached Ready for Review against 419 commits, and 163 of 288 background jobs failed. The single GPU lock was 92-94% busy, mostly with rebase, re-prove and merge attempts that failed. The design is in /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-ryannel-Workspace-thrum/e5ff9d25-dfb5-4b37-a169-158dbdac268c/scratchpad/proof-regime.md; section 4 has the steps T1a-T9. The script now does much of what it proposed: shared resources, lock hold limits, `reads`, a merge queue and main-branch checks with retry and bisect. Read ~/.claude/plugins/cache/ryannel-skills/orchestrate/2.3.1/skills/orchestration/build/SKILL.md, build-milestone/SKILL.md and plan-module/references/proofs.md before you change anything.

The owner's words, to quote wherever a change is the human's decision: "Ok, let's get the script and skill changes done then once we've got orchestrate to where it needs to be, let's get the lead on Thrum working." and "We want all these fixes in place before I head to bed tonight." The owner also confirmed "Go ahead" in the lead session on 15 Nov. That covered: a warning-only gate, an hourly verifier on main, `gpu: 2, chrome: 1`, BASELINE-GUARD re-planned, the rule and skill text updated, and accepting that an unintended image change can sit on main for about 2 hours.

Carry out, adjusted for 2.3.0:
- **T1a.** The exact-baselines gate in `./dev check` warns instead of refusing. Declare the verifier as a `Main-branch check` in ORCHESTRATE.md (every 1h; lock gpu; a timeout that fits the ~16 min run). Record a dated ruling in ARCHITECTURE.md's Exact baselines.
- **T1b.** The script now does the sentinel's shared run, retry, bisect and naming the culprit. Re-plan BASELINE-GUARD down to what remains Thrum's own (for example the verify command and the CPU ownership guard), and decide what happens to its in-flight M2 on branch build/baseline-guard.
- **Verifier items.** Open milestones carry about 116 items whose check runs `exact_baselines.py verify`. Changing `check` text resets progress, which `lock` and `reads` don't. Weigh repointing them at `python3 "$ORCHESTRATE_SCRIPT" main-check <name>` (no lock of its own) against having the verifier read the shared result. Pick the option that disturbs open branches least, and say why.
- **T2-T5,** as the report says. In T4, never nest gpu inside merge, and never hold a lock while waiting for a person.
- **T6.** Declare `Shared resources: gpu: 2, chrome: 1`; that capacity change is what ends most of the queueing. Give each item the lock its device needs for capacity. Use `gpu.alone` only for a run that needs the whole GPU, such as all its memory. It does not make timings trustworthy, because builders compiling elsewhere take no lock.
- **T9's timing policy is the timing fix.** Within a milestone, a timing item becomes a loose benchmark tripwire that catches a collapse. Precise numbers move to the module's last milestone, measured in one sitting with builders paused. Sweep the timing items to that line.
- **Fold T7-T8 in** where they're cheap; otherwise record them as later work.

The SCENE-VIEWS design review's Must Fix shared-height-map-camera-support came back after your last fix (docs/evidence/SCENE-VIEWS/design-review.md on origin/main). The design now admits every camera on the main camera's vertical but exempts some of them through a rounding exception, while M1.1, M2.1 and M1's quality bar still promise equality with the main view. Make the acceptance contract and the mechanism say the same thing: either remove the exception so every admitted camera really gets identical shadow products, or narrow the admitted range and the equality claims to exactly where they hold, and state the limit everywhere it applies (V1, V3, M1.1, M1.13, M2.1). Prefer the option that keeps water reflections correct at the least cost. Its Suggestions are yours to take or leave.

Plan the fix in the module that owns each test's code, as an item on its current milestone or as its next milestone, whichever lets it land soonest.
